results.title: Jenkins CI Pipeline with Python. Building a Jenkins CI Pipeline with… | by Joaquín Menchaca (智裕) | Medium
results.content: This is an introductory article about building and testing **Python** web api service with **Jenkins** CI (continuous integration) pipeline (using `Jenkinsfile`). * how to integrate this into **Jenkins**with JUnit test reporting support. ### Create the Tests. Run this in bash to create our test cases:. These tests will use a **xUnit** style of tests with the `unittest` library that comes bundled with the install of Python. In this example, we need to create a `setUp()` method that uses your instances of the `Flask` class, and call the `instance_name.app.test_client()`. As our instance is called `app` (from `app.py`), we will then use `app.app.test_client()`. The **test\_client** (`app.test_client()`) is a method provided the **Flask application object**, which creates a test client for the application. ### Running the Tests. Now that we have our web application and unit tests, we can create a **Jenkins** CI Pipeline by creating a `Jenkinsfile`. cat <<-'JENKINSFILE' > Jenkinsfilepipeline { agent { docker { image 'python:3.7.2' } } stages { stage('build') { steps { sh 'pip install -r requirements.txt' } } stage('test') { steps { sh 'python test.py' } } }}JENKINSFILE. For *build* and *test* stages, the pipeline will run a shell command, similar to have we have already ran in our previous steps, in the **Python** container. For this integration, we can use the **XMLRunner** library, and pass this as our test runner to the `unittest.main()` method. We need to update the `Jenkinsfile` to have a final *post* step in the *test* stage, that tells **Jenkins** where to find the **JUnit** test report. pipeline { agent { docker { image 'python:3.7.2' } } stages { stage('build') { steps { sh 'pip install -r requirements.txt' } } stage('test') { steps { sh 'python test.py' } post { always { junit 'test-reports/*.xml' } } } }}. In Jenkins, run this pipeline again, and you’ll see results under the Test link in the Blue Ocean interface. * Created Unit Tests with **JUnit** reporting integration. * Created a pipeline (`Jenkinsfile`) that will run the tests and provide visual feedback in Jenkins. * *Code commit to main or release branch*: when tests pass, push an artifact, such as pip package or docker image, or an artifact repository.

results.title: Run Cypress tests in Docker on Concourse CI | by Richard Forjoe
results.content: Published Time: 2022-01-03T17:48:15.074Z Run Cypress tests in Docker on Concourse CI Concourse is an open source tool for automating your software delivery pipeline. * Flexible, scalable and container based * Lightweight and easy to deploy * Pipelines and tasks are defined declaratively * Tasks use containers to easily control dependencies * Easily visualise pipelines in the Concourse dashboard * Supports any code anywhere, tested anyhow and deployed anywhere * Jobs run in parallel by default Having used Jenkins(legacy and doesn’t scale well), GitLab CI(loved), Github Actions(loved) and now Concourse CI, I’m finding it as a great tool, with similarities to GitLab CI but yet very different. See — Concourse CI has 3 main components: Web nodes, Worker nodes and a PostgresSQL node Before we dive in here are some useful links/learnings for where to learn more: * — main resource to get all the info you need * — great tutorial to get you started * — great article by Lindsay Auchinachie on Concourse UI * — VSCode plugin: Concourse CI Pipeline Editor Quick image of Concourse UI Each block is a pipeline, within each block are jobs and their status. Type ‘’fly -t <alias> login -c <concourse instance>’’ ci/resources/containers on  main ❯ fly -t training login -c logging in to team 'main'navigate to the following URL in your browser: enter token manually (input hidden): 4. 1. First step is going over the cypress pipeline e2e-test task in /ci/pipelines/cypress-pipeline.yml Here we are using the cypress docker image with tag 9.2.0: Under run attribute I’ve specified which cypress command to run. file>.yml -p <pipeline name> concourse-cypress/ci/pipelines on  main ❯ fly -t training set-pipeline -c cypress-pipeline.yml -p cypress-pipeline 3. * Update the pipeline resource to your repo and branch resources:- name: source-codetype: gitsource:uri: main So let’s go back to the basic building blocks of Concourse CI * **Tasks:** These do the fundamental work of the pipeline. This is where you pass in the pipeline resource needed by the task e.g. source-code which is the git repo being used which will be stored in the source-code folder * outputs: directory available to later steps in build plan * run: these are the shell script commands that will be executed.
